title: Z Combinator: Anonymous Recursion in Applicative Order
description: Defines Z combinator (strict Y variant) for applicative-order evaluation. Z = (lambda (f) ((lambda (x) (f (lambda (v) ((x x) v)))) (lambda (x) (f (lambda (v) ((x x) v)))))). Uses eta-expansion (lambda (v) ...) to delay self-application. fact = Z applied to recursive factorial function. (fact 6) evaluates to 720. Demonstrates recursion without define.
source: draft: omp free model + edit: codex

steps.description: Z combinator definition: takes f, applies (lambda (x) ...) to itself. Inner lambda takes x, returns (f (lambda (v) ((x x) v))). The eta-expanded (lambda (v) ...) delays (x x) until f needs it.
fact defined using Z: (Z (lambda (self) (lambda (n) (if (<= n 1) 1 (* n (self (- n 1))))))). self is the recursive call, provided by Z.

Key difference from eager Y: (lambda (v) ((x x) v)) wraps self-application in a lambda. In applicative order, argument (x x) would be evaluated immediately, causing infinite expansion. The lambda delays it: (x x) only runs when f calls its argument.

steps.question: Why does the eager Y combinator ((lambda (x) (f (x x))) (lambda (x) (f (x x)))) diverge under applicative-order evaluation?
steps.answer: Applicative order evaluates arguments before applying. Applying (lambda (x) (f (x x))) to itself receives a lambda argument that is already a value. But the body (f (x x)) tries to evaluate (x x), repeating self-application in an infinite loop. Z's eta-expansion makes the argument a function, not a self-application.
